title: What Genes Do
body:
Genes are segments of DNA that carry instructions for building proteins and regulating when those proteins are made, and together with environment and chance they shape how a body grows, works, and responds to the world.

Real genetics context: a human genome holds about twenty thousand protein-coding genes, plus regulatory DNA that switches genes on and off, and most traits arise from many genes together, not one gene alone. Limits: a gene's effect depends on other genes, on environment, and on development, so no single gene predicts a whole person.

Labeled speculative fiction: a story in which one gene is switched to grant a superpower is fiction, not genetics. This record gives no instructions for human genetic modification, no DIY gene-editing instructions, and no protocols for editing human DNA. Any speculation in it is labeled fictional, and the genetics described are observed variation and research context, not a recipe.

title: Heritability of Height
body:
Height is highly heritable: children of tall parents tend to be tall, and twin studies put height's heritability near eighty percent, yet height still varies within families and across populations.

Real genetics context: hundreds of genetic variants each add or subtract millimeters, and nutrition, health, and childhood environment shift the result by centimeters, which is why height is a distribution, not a destiny. Limits: no gene or small set of genes determines height alone, and heritability is a population statistic, not a personal prediction.

Labeled speculative fiction: a story in which height is dialed to a chosen value is fiction. This record gives no instructions for human genetic modification, no DIY gene-editing instructions, and no protocols for editing human DNA. title: Eye Color Variation
body:
Eye color varies from brown to green to blue and grey, and the variation comes mainly from how much melanin the iris makes and how light scatters in its layers, not from a single eye-color gene.

Real genetics context: several genes, notably those controlling melanin production and transport, shape eye color, and the result is a continuum with common categories, which is why two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child. Limits: eye color predicts nothing about character, ability, or health beyond a few linked conditions.

title: Lactose Tolerance Variation
body:
Lactose tolerance in adulthood varies by ancestry: many people stop making the lactase enzyme after childhood, while others, notably in populations with long dairy-herding histories, keep making it for life.

Real genetics context: a regulatory variant near the lactase gene keeps the gene switched on in adults, and its spread tracks the history of milk drinking, a clear case of culture and genetics interacting. Limits: tolerance is a digestive trait, not a general superiority, and intolerance is the common human condition, managed by diet.

title: Muscle Fiber Types
body:
Human muscle holds two broad fiber families: slow fibers built for endurance and fast fibers built for power, and the mix a person is born with leans them toward endurance or sprinting, though training shifts performance within that range.

Real genetics context: a well-studied variant in the ACTN3 gene affects fast-fiber protein, and elite sprinters and endurance athletes differ in fiber mix on average, yet training, coaching, and opportunity matter as much as any variant. Limits: no variant makes an athlete, and fiber mix is one factor among many.

Labeled speculative fiction: a story in which fiber type is rewritten to grant superhuman speed or strength is fiction. title: Blood Types
body:
Blood types describe antigens on red blood cells, the ABO system and the Rh factor chief among them, and they matter for safe transfusion, for pregnancy, and for a few disease risks, but not for personality or ability.

Real genetics context: ABO types are inherited by simple rules from parental types, and Rh status follows its own gene, which is why blood type is a classic teaching example of inheritance. Limits: blood type does not determine diet, character, or talent, despite popular claims to the contrary.

title: Sickle Cell Trait and Disease
body:
Sickle cell disease comes from a variant in the hemoglobin gene that, in two copies, distorts red blood cells into sickle shapes, causing pain, anemia, and organ damage, while one copy, the trait, usually causes few symptoms and historically protected against malaria.

Real genetics context: this is the textbook case of a variant that is harmful in two copies and protective in one, in malarial regions, which is why it persists in populations despite its cost. Limits: the trait is not a general advantage, and the disease is a serious medical condition managed by clinical care, not by this record.

Labeled speculative fiction: a story in which a blood variant grants invulnerability or another power is fiction, and it would be wrong to romanticize a serious disease. title: Taste Sensitivity (PTC)
body:
Taste sensitivity varies: some people taste the compound PTC as intensely bitter, others taste little or nothing, and the difference comes from variants in a taste-receptor gene, a classic example of sensory genetics.

Real genetics context: tasters, non-tasters, and medium tasters form a spectrum, and the same receptor family shapes responses to many bitter foods, which is why taste preference runs in families without being a matter of willpower. Limits: taste sensitivity predicts food preference only weakly, and it says nothing about general ability.

title: Red Hair Variation
body:
Red hair comes from variants in the MC1R gene that shift melanin production from dark eumelanin toward red pheomelanin, producing red hair, fair skin, and freckles in many carriers, with wide variation in shade.

Real genetics context: MC1R variants also affect sun sensitivity and, in research, aspects of pain response and anesthesia, but they do not determine personality or talent. Limits: red hair is one visible trait among thousands of variants, and most carriers have no MC1R-related medical condition.

Labeled speculative fiction: a story in which red hair grants fire powers is fiction, and this record does not link hair color to any ability. title: Skin Tone Variation
body:
Skin tone varies continuously across humanity, from very light to very dark, and the variation comes from melanin amount and type, shaped by many genes and by the history of sunlight exposure in ancestral populations.

Real genetics context: melanin protects against ultraviolet damage and, in balance, allows vitamin D production, which is why skin tone tracks historical sunlight, and the variation is continuous, not a set of separate kinds. Limits: skin tone predicts nothing about ability, character, or worth, and it is described here only as biology.

title: Twin Studies
body:
Twin studies compare identical twins, who share nearly all their DNA, with fraternal twins, who share about half, to estimate how much of a trait's variation in a population comes from genes versus environment.

Real genetics context: twin studies have informed heritability estimates for height, weight, cognition, and many medical traits, and they work because twins share wombs, families, and eras, which must be accounted for in any reading. Limits: heritability is a population number that changes with environment, and identical twins still differ, which is itself evidence that genes are not destiny.

Labeled speculative fiction: a story in which twins share thoughts or powers by genetics is fiction. title: Natural Athletic Variation
body:
Natural athletic variation means people differ in build, fiber mix, lung capacity, coordination, and recovery, and those differences, together with training and opportunity, shape who reaches elite sport, without any single variant deciding it.

Real genetics context: elite athletes differ from the general population on many small variants at once, and the same variant set appears in non-athletes too, which is why genetics alone never identifies a champion. Limits: training, coaching, nutrition, health, and access matter as much as, or more than, any gene.

title: Aging and Telomeres (General)
body:
Telomeres are protective caps on chromosome ends that shorten as cells divide, and their length is associated, in population research, with aging and with some disease risks, though the relationship is complex and not a simple clock.

Real genetics context: telomere length is influenced by genes, stress, smoking, and disease, and it is studied as a marker, not a master switch, of aging. Limits: telomere length does not predict an individual's lifespan, and lengthening telomeres is not a proven or safe anti-aging therapy.

title: Immune Diversity (HLA)
body:
Immune diversity comes largely from the HLA genes, which present fragments of invaders to the immune system, and their extraordinary variety means different people recognize different threats well, which is why populations survive plagues that kill individuals.

Real genetics context: HLA matching matters for organ and stem-cell transplants, and HLA types are associated with autoimmune risks, which is why diversity itself is the protection, not any single type. Limits: no HLA type makes a person generally invulnerable, and immune strength is a balance, since overactivity causes autoimmune disease.

Labeled speculative fiction: a story in which an immune type grants immunity to all disease is fiction. title: Circadian Rhythm Variation
body:
Circadian rhythm variation means people differ in their internal clocks: morning types wake early and fade early, evening types wake late and peak late, and the difference is partly genetic, partly age, and partly habit and light exposure.

Real genetics context: clock genes run a roughly twenty-four-hour cycle in nearly every cell, and variants shift its timing, which is why sleep timing runs in families and why teenagers shift later. Limits: rhythm type is a preference and a timing, not a measure of worth or ability, and light and schedule can shift it within limits.

Labeled speculative fiction: a story in which a clock gene grants sleeplessness or time powers is fiction. title: Memory and Learning Variation (General)
body:
Memory and learning vary between people, and that variation comes from many genes, from brain development, from sleep, from schooling, and from practice, with no single gene determining intelligence or memory.

Real genetics context: cognitive traits are among the most polygenic traits known, with thousands of variants each contributing tiny effects, and environment, especially education and health, shifts outcomes substantially. Limits: no genetic test measures a person's intelligence, potential, or worth, and this record makes no such claim.

Labeled speculative fiction: a story in which memory or intelligence is granted by a gene is fiction.
